prompt: Match each verb to what it does to a resource.
hint: The table in the section.

pairs.right: Makes the item exactly the body sent

prompt: A script gets `503 Service Unavailable` from a device. What does the first digit tell it?
hint: 4 or 5?

choices.text: The request was wrong and will fail again unchanged
choices.why: That is a 4xx.

choices.text: The server failed; it could work later
choices.why: Right. A 5xx is the server's problem.

choices.text: The token expired
choices.why: That is a 401.

choices.text: It worked, with a warning
choices.why: Success is 2xx.

prompt: In the answer to `curl -si …/system`, where is the status code?
hint: Before the headers.

choices.text: In the body, as a field called `status`
choices.why: The body here held an `error` field and no status.

choices.text: On the first line, `HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: In the `WWW-Authenticate` header
choices.why: That header says which credentials the server wants.

choices.text: After the blank line
choices.why: After the blank line comes the body.

prompt: The header that says the body of an answer is JSON is `___: application/json`.
hint: It names the type of the content.

prompt: Why does the lesson build `login.json` with `jq` from `~/.netops-password` instead of typing the password in the `curl` command?
hint: Where does a command line end up?

choices.text: It lands in the shell history and the process list
choices.why: Right. Both can be read by others.

choices.text: `curl` refuses any password longer than eight characters
choices.why: It has no such limit.

choices.text: JSON cannot be typed by hand
choices.why: It can; the wrong-password example did.

choices.text: The router accepts files and refuses strings
choices.why: The router receives the same bytes either way.

prompt: The `audit` account's `PATCH` was answered `403`, not `401`. What does that difference mean?
hint: Who you are, against what you may do.

choices.text: The token had expired
choices.why: An expired token is a 401.

choices.text: It knew who asked and refused the action
choices.why: Right: authenticated, not authorised.

choices.text: The interface name was wrong for this account
choices.why: The same token read `eth2` a line earlier.

choices.text: The server was overloaded and asked for a retry
choices.why: That is a 429 or a 503.

prompt: A login answers a wrong password and an unknown username with the same `401` and the same sentence. Why is that the right design?
hint: What would a stranger learn from two different answers?

choices.text: It keeps the code of the API shorter
choices.why: Brevity is not the reason.

choices.text: HTTP forbids two different messages for a 401
choices.why: It does not; the body is free.

choices.text: Two answers would tell a stranger which usernames exist
choices.why: Right. That is half of what an attacker needs.

choices.text: Clients would misread two sentences
choices.why: A client reads the status code first.

prompt: The login answered `"expires_in": 900`. For how many minutes is the token valid?
hint: The value is in seconds.

prompt: Every request after the login carries the token in the header `Authorization: ___ <token>`.
hint: Whoever bears it is trusted.

prompt: A script calls `requests.get(url)` without `timeout=`. The device accepts the connection and never answers. What happens?
hint: What is the default timeout of `requests`?

choices.text: It gives up after 30 seconds
choices.why: There is no default timeout.

choices.text: The script waits indefinitely
choices.why: Right, which is why every call here gives one.

choices.text: `requests` raises an `HTTPError`
choices.why: No status code ever arrives to raise on.

choices.text: It retries three times and then raises
choices.why: That is `Device.request` for a 429, not `requests` itself.

prompt: `login.py` without `raise_for_status()` gets a `401`. Where does the script fail?
hint: `requests` hands back a 401 like any other answer.

choices.text: At `r.json()["token"]`, with a `KeyError` that hides the real cause
choices.why: Right. The body had `error`, not `token`.

choices.text: At `requests.post`, which raises for any 4xx
choices.why: It does not raise by itself.

choices.text: It does not fail; it prints the system facts anyway
choices.why: No token, no facts.

choices.text: At the `import requests` line
choices.why: The import has nothing to do with the answer.

prompt: Which things does `devapi.Device` keep so that each script does not repeat them? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at the constructor.

choices.text: The base address of the API
choices.why: Yes, `self.base`.

choices.text: The certificate authority to verify against
choices.why: Yes, `self.http.verify`.

choices.text: The token, in the session's headers
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The password, for each request
choices.why: It is read once, for the login, and not kept.

prompt: The same `POST` to `/static-routes` was sent twice. What did the second one get?
hint: The route was already there.

choices.text: `201 Created`, and a second copy
choices.why: The server refused to duplicate it.

choices.text: `409 Conflict`
choices.why: Right, with the address of the existing route.

choices.text: `200 OK`, and nothing changed
choices.why: That is how the `PUT` in `static.py` behaves when nothing differs.

choices.text: `422 Unprocessable Entity`
choices.why: The body was valid.

prompt: In the address `/static-routes/192.0.2.128%2F25`, the characters `%2F` stand for the character ___.
hint: It separates parts of a path.

prompt: A script must make sure a static route exists with distance 10, and may run many times. Which request fits best?
hint: Which verb is idempotent and names the item?

choices.text: `POST` to `/static-routes`, and ignore a 409 if the route is already there
choices.why: A 409 would hide a route that exists with the wrong distance.

choices.text: `PUT` to `/static-routes/192.0.2.128%2F25` with the whole route
choices.why: Right. It creates or replaces, and repeating it changes nothing.

choices.text: `DELETE` then `POST`, every time
choices.why: It removes a working route for a moment on every run.

choices.text: `PATCH` to `/static-routes`
choices.why: The collection does not accept `PATCH`.

prompt: `192.0.2.130/25` was refused with `422`. What was wrong with it?
hint: Compare it with the network a /25 starting at .128 would be.

choices.text: Its host bits are set
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The JSON was malformed
choices.why: Malformed JSON would be a 400; this was valid JSON.

choices.text: /25 is not allowed for static routes on FRR
choices.why: `192.0.2.128/25` was accepted earlier.

choices.text: The next hop is unreachable
choices.why: The same next hop was accepted with the right prefix.

prompt: Match each answer from the lesson to what caused it.
hint: One cause per code.

prompt: A page arrives with `"count": 4`, two results and `"next": null`. What should the client conclude?
hint: Which field decides whether to ask again?

choices.text: It has the last page and should stop
choices.why: Right. `next` decides, not arithmetic.

choices.text: Two items are missing, so it should ask for offset=2
choices.why: If this is the last page, the other two came earlier.

choices.text: The server is broken and the client should retry
choices.why: Nothing here is an error.

choices.text: It should ask again with a bigger limit, to fetch the whole list at once
choices.why: It already has everything.

prompt: An API changes from offset pagination to cursor pagination, keeping the `next` field. Which client keeps working?
hint: Which client built addresses itself?

choices.text: The one that adds `limit` to `offset` for each page
choices.why: There is no offset any more.

choices.text: The one that follows `next` until it is null
choices.why: Right, like `Device.all`.

choices.text: The one that asks for `limit=100000`
choices.why: This API caps limit at 100, and a large page is not a strategy.

choices.text: Neither of them survives the change
choices.why: The one that followed links does not notice.

prompt: A list has 125 items and the client uses `limit=50`. How many requests does it take to read the whole list?
hint: The last page is not full.

prompt: In the pagination style of the lab's API and of NetBox, the query parameter that says how many items to skip is called ___.
hint: It sits beside `limit` in every `next` link.

prompt: What does `429 Too Many Requests` with `Retry-After: 8` ask the client to do?
hint: The header is a number of seconds.

choices.text: Log in again
choices.why: The token is fine; the rate is not.

choices.text: Wait eight seconds and send the same request again
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Give up: 4xx means the request is wrong
choices.why: 429 is the 4xx where retrying after a wait is right.

choices.text: Retry at once on another connection
choices.why: The limit is per token, not per connection.

prompt: A colleague makes `Device.request` retry every 4xx after a pause. What goes wrong when the password changes?
hint: What does a 401 become if it is retried?

choices.text: The router locks the account after three attempts
choices.why: This router does not; and it is not the lesson's point.

choices.text: It retries in vain and hides the real cause
choices.why: Right. A 401 needs a person, not a pause.

choices.text: Nothing: the retries eventually get a 200
choices.why: A wrong password stays wrong.

choices.text: The token is refreshed by the retries
choices.why: Retries send the same request, with the same token.

prompt: The routers allow 30 requests in any 10 seconds per token. At most how many requests per minute can one token sustain?
hint: Six windows of ten seconds.

prompt: Which habits keep a script from meeting a device's rate limit? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three are in the section.

choices.text: Reuse one session and log in once
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Ask for a page of many items rather than many requests for one
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Spread start times with a small random delay
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Open a new connection for each request
choices.why: That costs the device more, not less.

choices.text: Retry immediately when refused
choices.why: That is the opposite of waiting.

prompt: `curl -sS https://edge1.example.net/…` without `--cacert` exits with status 60. Why?
hint: Who issued the router's certificate?

choices.text: The router's certificate has expired since the lab was built
choices.why: The same certificate verified with the lab's authority.

choices.text: `ctl` does not know the issuer
choices.why: Right. `--cacert lab-ca.pem` supplies it.

choices.text: The API does not speak HTTPS
choices.why: It does; the handshake is what failed.

choices.text: A password was missing
choices.why: TLS fails before any HTTP request is sent.

prompt: A script against an internal device fails with `CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED`. Which fix is right?
hint: One of these makes the error go away by checking nothing.

choices.text: `verify=False`
choices.why: It sends the password to whoever answers.

choices.text: Point `requests` at the issuing authority's file
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Switch the script to plain `http://`
choices.why: That removes encryption as well as the check.

choices.text: Silence the warning `requests` prints
choices.why: The warning is the symptom, not the problem.

prompt: In the `openssl s_client` output, what does `Verify return code: 0 (ok)` mean?
hint: Zero is how programs say success.

choices.text: The chain checked out against `lab-ca.pem`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The connection used no encryption at any point
choices.why: It is TLS.

choices.text: Zero certificates were sent
choices.why: One was, for `edge1.example.net`.

choices.text: The API returned an empty body to the request
choices.why: `s_client` sent no HTTP request.

prompt: Put the steps of `static.py` in the order it runs them.
hint: Credentials first, the decision last.
items: Log in and keep the token
List the static routes, page by page
Compare the route with the wanted one

prompt: A monitoring script reads interfaces every minute from 300 routers. Which account should its token belong to?
hint: What is the worst a leaked token could do?

choices.text: `netops`, because it can do everything the script might need later
choices.why: A leak would then allow changes on 300 routers.

choices.text: A read-only account like `audit`
choices.why: Right. Reading is all it does.

choices.text: A new account per router
choices.why: Accounts per router do not limit what each can do.

choices.text: Whichever account has the longest token lifetime
choices.why: A longer life makes a leak worse.
